newsitem.title: UK: BT dives, can't rule out new MCI deal.
newsitem.headline: BT dives, can't rule out new MCI deal.

text.p: British Telecommunications Plc said on Friday it could not rule out renegotiating a $24 billion merger with MCI after America's second biggest long-distance carrier issued a profit warning.

As BT's shares plunged by close to 10 percent, a BT spokesman said the group was looking at what he described as a "complex situation". MCI announced late on Thursday that losses due to heavy investments in local markets would be more than twice forecasts this year.
MCI said local market losses for this year could reach $800 million -- and losses in 1998 in its local business could exceed those of this year.
But the BT spokesman said it was too soon to draw any conclusions about the planned merger. "At this stage, we are simply looking at the figures and anything beyond that is premature," he said.

Shares in BT went into free-fall before stabilising at 437p, a loss of 40.5p. Around 170 million shares had exchanged hand by 1540 GMT in frantic trade -- the highest daily total since BT was floated in 1984.
But although some analysts scaled back profit forecasts, trade in BT options mainly saw traders buying calls in the hopes that the stock will bounce.
In New York, MCI shares fell around $6.0 to $36-3/8.
Some Wall Street takeover experts said BT might pare back the price it was paying for MCI.

But most analysts in London -- and concerned and exhausted MCI shareholders from across the Atlantic who had been awake all night watching developments -- said they thought it unlikely that BT would renegotiate a deal it has consistently hailed as a great strategic acquisition since announcing it last November.
"I think any renegotiation...would be a loss of face and more importantly damage confidence in BT's ability to deliver strategic goals," said Andrew Harrington, telecoms analyst at Salomon Brothers.

Another analyst, who declined to be named, noted that MCI was a technology leader which unlike BT had not been focused on shareholder returns, but agreed that any renegotiation of the merger was unlikely.

"On balance it would be seen as too much of an about-face and I think BT would be up for a lot of criticism if a telecoms company of their stature did not understand the difficulties of local loop (markets)," she said. "One must assume BT invested with their eyes fully open."
MCI blamed higher-than-expected losses related to delays by U.S. regional telecoms companies, which dominate the local market, in opening the industry to long-distance rivals.

As alarmed MCI shareholders attempted to second-guess BT's next move, concerns were raised that MCI might be blaming a slacking of its general business on a poor performance of its local operations. Others said MCI might be exaggerating its losses to push U.S. regulators into opening up local markets faster.
"It's a tough call to predict," said one MCI investor. "Right now the bet is that this deal happens. This might just be posturing on MCI's part."
The U.S. Telecommunications Reform Act of 1996 established a framework for local and long distance companies to enter each other's markets.
But MCI says its ability to expand its local-service offerings depends largely on regulators restricting local monopolies from "thwarting competition".
BT's chief executive Sir Peter Bonfield backed MCI's calls for the effective opening of the U.S. telecoms markets, reassuring on some worries that the strategies of the two firms had parted company.
Bonfield urged a proactive approach to regulation to be adopted throughout the world, especially in the U.S. "which so often provides the lead for others to follow".

Robert Fleming is one broker which has been consistently cautious about BT's insistence that its deal with MCI to create a new company, Concert Plc, will yield "tremendous growth prospects". The broker notes that the U.S. market has one of the lowest returns and has questioned whether Concert can raise dividends by the promised six percent per year for the forseeable future.
However, Salomon Brothers' Harrington said although growth expectations for Concert in the next three or four years were too high, investing in MCI made sense.

"The strategy (of investing in local markets) makes a huge amount of sense. BT support it, we support it, (but) the cost is going to be a lot higher and the dilution to BT shareholders is going to be a lot higher than people thought," he said.

Harrington believes that amid a jostling of telecoms giants to form global alliances and win high-margin contracts from multinational customers, BT's plan to merge with MCI secures its long-term prosperity.
